posts.title: A Summer at Microsoft — Data Flywheel Team
posts.excerpt: Notes from a summer internship on Microsoft's Data Flywheel team: building an LLM-powered bug triage system for Word, restarting a project six weeks in, and learning where to draw the line between model judgment and deterministic code.
posts.content:
I spent May through August 2026 in Redmond, Washington as a software engineering intern on Microsoft's Data Flywheel team with Word. I still recall getting the offer in October 2025, overjoyed. It was an incredible opportunity, and hearing I would be directly involved in incorporating Copilot into Microsoft Word was so thrilling. Being in a new city, on a gorgeous campus full of so many other incredible engineers made me feel, for the first time in a long time, sheer excitement for getting to build, code, and problem-solve.

Here's how it went, roughly in order.

May: the wrong problem

After usual introductions and understanding the team, things were clear: this was a very new team. And with this came a lot more flexibility, and with that, responsibility to carve my own path. Compared to just handling tickets and building features, my role demanded more innovation. This realization was confirmed with my task: make the triaging process for crash spikes faster. This was a very unique situation, as most of my other intern friends' projects had a very different nature to them. Needless to say, the first stretch was misaligned. I was building toward a problem framing that didn't match what the team needed, and by the time that became clear, the project had to be restarted more or less from the top. Naturally, this was super frustrating, seeing what felt like progress tumble in one meeting. It was an uncomfortable place to be five weeks (roughly end of June) into a twelve-week internship, hitting the reset button. It's also, I'd argue, the single most useful thing that happened all summer, because everything after it was shaped by having gotten it wrong once.

The correction was mostly about scope. I had been thinking of the system as something I would design; the useful version was something that would extend infrastructure the team already ran. Microsoft already ran a standardized Reliability AI agent, but it didn't really deliver on its own. It became clear the right move was to build onto it rather than around it.

June: telemetry and the shape of the data

Word's crash telemetry arrives through Kusto and OpenTelemetry. There's also a product called Watson that collects related crashes into "buckets," which helps with classification. Before anything intelligent can be layered on top, you have to understand what a "crash spike" actually is in that data, and deeply at that — how noisy the signal is, how spikes cluster, how much of the volume is a handful of recurring failure modes versus a long tail. After all, to build an agent smart enough to automate triage, I needed to be capable of doing the same thing manually, at least to a large extent.

With this in mind, the rest of June was prototyping. I first spent a lot of time mirroring my manager and the other reliability engineers, learning how they triage a spike by hand. Then I wrote my own design doc for how the system would work, largely for my own sake. After that, I built out the agent's glossary, so it actually knew Word's crash terminology, what databases were conventionally used, and what the different columns really meant. From there, after a lot of manual runs and experimentation, I settled on a set of prompts to work from.

July: LLM judgment vs. deterministic heuristics

July is when it started to look like a real system. I added more sub-agents, and it could send emails and report back properly. The feedback I was getting was solid; on old crash spikes, the agent was starting to make the same diagnoses within five minutes that would take engineers a whole day to push through. Seeing these results after the May reset felt really good — it felt like I was finally on the right track.

In parallel, I made six manual fixes that together addressed over 50,000 crashes and hangs, using help from the agent I was building. It was incredibly rewarding to see some of that work get pushed into the Word codebase, even if it was only small pieces.

Throughout: actually shipping fixes

I also spent time with the NLX team on Word's proof checker (the spell and grammar checker). There was a bug in how multi-word expressions (MWEs) were suggested — it failed to recognize that typing one word of the expression should surface a suggestion for the rest of it. The fix was a filter at the suggestion layer rather than something deeper in the pipeline: we built a small vocabulary of MWEs to reference, then checked their individual parts and surrounding context before returning suggestions. Validation included a Hungarian-language audit, which was a nice excuse to use a language I actually speak in a place where it mattered; I found and logged a few concerns in the Hungarian proof-checker along the way.

Alongside the agent work, I added to Word's internal documentation — a wiki page about the new AI tool and how some of the internal Copilot infrastructure works, since I'd ended up close to it. I also documented my own onboarding process, which turned into a new onboarding guide for the team since the last one was a few years out of date.

August: the unsanctioned version

The last two weeks were the final presentation push, and they were probably the most valuable two weeks of the whole internship.

Partly because I made another mistake: poor code-cycle control. I had one giant draft PR that was too big to review or iterate on as a single unit, so I broke it down into a large number of smaller PRs. That took surgical splitting — making sure each one worked standalone — and then addressing feedback on each immediately. Doing that taught me how to iterate much faster; I ended up pushing more code into the codebase in those two weeks than in the rest of the summer combined.

Those last two weeks also made me realize how far out of my shell I had to come. Continuously shipping, collaborating, asking for things — that didn't come automatically to me. I spent a lot of time worrying about mistakes, about what others would think, about bothering people. Those two weeks were genuinely uncomfortable: I was regularly pestering engineers for PR reviews and making embarrassing mistakes along the way. And despite that, I didn't get a single complaint or any sense of judgment, which told me a lot about how much I'd been holding myself back. My work still made it into the internal Copilot package, which I was glad to pull off.

What I'd take away

"Use an LLM" is not a design. The interesting work for me was drawing the line between what the model decides and what your code decides, and defending that line — and from there, figuring out how to build around that engine to fit into infrastructure that already existed. That turns out to be a real engineering question in its own right.

I learned a lot this summer. My manager was harsh, and honestly I could rarely relate to my fellow interns when they described their own experiences. I came to learn that my happiness wasn't something I could sustainably tie to my work, which became clear under the pressure from my team. But I don't want to frame that as bad blood — in retrospect, it feels more sweet than bitter, given how much it taught me about what it means to be a great engineer rather than just a good one. My philosophy as a developer was broadened a lot this summer, and I'm leaving better for it.

Thanks to the Data Flywheel and NLX teams for the summer.

posts.title: Welcome to My Blog
posts.excerpt: Starting a blog to share updates on projects, learning experiences, and other interesting things I'm working on.
posts.content:
Welcome to my blog! I'm starting this as a way to document my journey in computer science, machine learning, and software engineering.

Here I'll share updates on projects I'm working on, things I'm learning, and other interesting developments in my work and studies.
